opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. Doug's group was quite unusual for its time. In the 1980s, much of AI was focused either on expert systems, encoding lots of domain knowledge as rules, or on logic-based approaches to reasoning. And there was the resurgence of neural networks with the PDP work. Doug was interested in something different: what he saw as the core of intelligence, which is analogy-making and high-level perception, the ability to see one situation as being like another, to perceive the essence of a situation and recognize it in a very different context.

He chose to study this in deliberately simple, idealized microdomains. My thesis project, Copycat, worked on letter-string analogies like "if abc changes to abd, what does ijk change to?" People found that strange. Why would you work on these toy problems when others were building systems for medical diagnosis or chess? But Doug's view was that these little domains captured the essential issues of conceptual fluidity: how concepts stretch and slip, how context shapes what you perceive, how you balance competing pressures to arrive at an interpretation. He wanted to strip away the need for vast world knowledge so we could focus on the mechanisms themselves.

The architecture was also different. It wasn't a top-down search or a pure symbolic rule system, and it wasn't a standard neural network either. It was a stochastic, parallel architecture inspired partly by things like ant colonies and the immune system, with many small agents, which we called codelets, exploring possibilities simultaneously, and a network of concepts whose activations shifted as the system perceived the problem. Perception and reasoning were intertwined rather than separate stages, and the system's temperature reflected how coherent its current understanding was.

So the focus was less on performance on some benchmark and more on cognitive modeling, trying to understand how something like human understanding could emerge from lower-level processes. That made us outliers, and in some ways the questions we were asking, about abstraction, analogy, and what it really means to understand, are ones the field is coming back to now.

r003.rationale: It contrasts application-oriented systems with the group’s emphasis on cognitive modeling and understanding how human-like understanding emerges.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, when I joined Doug's group in the mid-1980s, most of AI was really focused on what you might call the symbolic approach. People were building expert systems, logic-based reasoning systems, things where you'd hand-code knowledge in the form of rules and then have the system do inference over those rules. And the neural network revival was just starting to happen at the same time, with the connectionists, so there was this emerging split between symbolic AI and neural networks.

Doug's group was sort of orthogonal to both of those. What Doug was interested in, and what I became interested in, was the question of how concepts work in the mind. How do we form concepts? How do we recognize that one situation is similar to another? How do we make analogies? And his view was that analogy-making isn't some special, high-level, exotic kind of reasoning that you do occasionally. It's really at the core of all of cognition. Every time you recognize something as an instance of a concept, you're making an analogy of a kind.

So the focus was on building computer models that captured that fluidity of concepts. The idea that concepts aren't rigid, that they have what Doug called "halos" of related concepts around them, and that they can slip into one another under pressure. We were working in these very idealized microdomains, like letter-string analogy problems, which is what my thesis project, Copycat, was about. And a lot of people in mainstream AI thought those were toy problems that weren't going to lead anywhere. But our view was that you had to understand these mechanisms in a simple domain before you could hope to scale them up.

The other thing that was different was the emphasis on the architecture itself. We weren't doing search over a space of possibilities in the traditional AI sense, and we weren't training a network on lots of data. We were trying to build something that was partly bottom-up and partly top-down, with lots of parallel, probabilistic, somewhat stochastic agents interacting, which was inspired by things like the immune system and ant colonies. So in a way it was a kind of emergent computation, but with explicit concepts in it. That combination, I think, was pretty unusual at the time, and honestly it still is.

r001.rationale: The response focuses on concepts and cognition in the human mind, but does not identify intelligence beyond individual human intelligence as a research focus.

r002.rationale: It says analogy-making is at the core of cognition and describes studying how people make analogies.

r003.rationale: It describes modeling concepts and understanding mechanisms in simple domains, but does not state that understanding intelligence took priority over building AI for particular applications.

r004.rationale: The response discusses concepts and cognition, but does not identify cognitive science as an influence defining the group’s approach relative to other AI research.

astra-6.text:
The focus in Doug’s group was on analogy as a central part of intelligence. And by analogy, I don’t just mean solving questions like “A is to B as C is to what?” I mean our ability to recognize that a new situation is like something we’ve encountered before, even when the surface details are very different, and to use that connection to make sense of it.

A lot of AI at the time focused on encoding knowledge and rules for reasoning in a particular domain. We were more interested in how you arrive at the right concepts in the first place. How do you decide what matters in a situation? How does your interpretation change as you notice something new?

That was the motivation behind Copycat, the project I worked on with Doug. We studied analogies in a very simple world of letter strings. The point wasn’t that letter strings were an important practical application. It was that, even in this tiny world, you could study the interplay between perception and concepts—how a system could flexibly reinterpret a situation rather than just apply a fixed rule. So the emphasis was really on understanding the mechanisms of human thought.

r002.rationale: It explicitly says analogy was central to the group’s focus and describes recognizing and using similarities across situations.

r003.rationale: It contrasts the group’s aim of understanding flexible thought with domain-specific AI and says the project was not intended as a practical application.

sol-6.1.text:
In Doug’s group, we were really focused on analogy as a core part of intelligence. And by analogy, I don’t just mean the kinds of problems you might see on a standardized test. I mean the ability to recognize that a new situation is like something you’ve experienced before, and to understand what matters about that similarity.

A lot of AI at the time focused on representing knowledge explicitly and building rules for reasoning with it. We were interested in how you arrive at the right representation in the first place. How do concepts adapt to a particular situation? How do you decide which features are relevant? Doug saw those processes as central to thinking, rather than as something you could assume had already been done.

That led us to work on very small, idealized domains, where we could study those questions closely. The ambition was to understand the mechanisms underlying flexible thought, even if the system itself was working on a very simple task.
